summary: Reviewed the entire dvpwa (Damn Vulnerable Python Web Application) Python codebase including routes, views, data access objects, templates, and configuration. This is an intentionally vulnerable educational application. Found 7 high-confidence security vulnerabilities spanning SQL injection, stored XSS, weak cryptography, session fixation, disabled CSRF protection, broken access control, and hardcoded credentials. All findings are directly exploitable through the web application.

findings.title: SQL Injection in Student Creation
findings.description: User-supplied student name is directly concatenated into SQL query using string formatting, allowing attackers to inject arbitrary SQL commands. An attacker can append SQL injection payloads (e.g., `Robert'); DROP TABLE students CASCADE; --`) to the student name field to execute arbitrary database operations.
findings.evidence:
```python
@staticmethod
async def create(conn: Connection, name: str):
    q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) "
         "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})
    async with conn.cursor() as cur:
        await cur.execute(q)
```
The `name` parameter from user input is interpolated directly into the query string before being sent to the database.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries with the database driver's built-in parameter handling. Replace the string interpolation with proper parameter placeholders: `q = "INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%s)"; await cur.execute(q, (name,))`

findings.title: Stored XSS via Disabled Jinja2 Auto-Escaping
findings.description: Jinja2 template auto-escaping is explicitly disabled, allowing stored XSS attacks. Attackers can inject JavaScript through any user-controlled fields (student names, course descriptions, reviews) that are displayed in templates. When these pages are rendered, the malicious JavaScript executes in the browser context of any user viewing the page.
findings.evidence:
```python
setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli', 'templates'),
            context_processors=[csrf_processor, auth_user_processor],
            autoescape=False)  # VULNERABLE: Auto-escaping disabled
```
Combined with template rendering like `{{ review.review_text }}` in course.jinja2:22 and `{{ student.name }}` in students.jinja2:16, user input is rendered as raw HTML/JavaScript.
findings.recommendation: Change `autoescape=False` to `autoescape=True` or remove the parameter (True is the default in Jinja2). This will automatically escape all variable content in templates. For intentional HTML content, use Jinja2's `|safe` filter sparingly after explicitly sanitizing with a library like `bleach`.

findings.title: Weak Cryptographic Hashing for Password Storage
findings.description: Passwords are hashed using MD5 without salt. MD5 is cryptographically broken, fast to brute-force, and has numerous rainbow tables available online. Attackers can easily recover plaintext passwords by: (1) Brute-forcing the MD5 hash (billions of common passwords per second), (2) Using rainbow tables, (3) Analyzing hash patterns (identical passwords produce identical hashes, revealing password reuse). This enables credential compromise with trivial computational effort.
findings.recommendation: Use a dedicated password hashing algorithm like argon2, bcrypt, or pbkdf2. Example: `from argon2 import PasswordHasher; ph = PasswordHasher(); hash = ph.hash(password); verified = ph.verify(hash, password_input)`. Never use MD5, SHA1, or unsalted hashing for passwords.

findings.title: Session Fixation via Accessible Session Cookie
findings.description: Session cookie is created with `httponly=False`, allowing JavaScript to access it via `document.cookie`. An attacker can: (1) Fix a user's session by injecting their own session ID, (2) Read the session cookie with JavaScript, (3) Perform session hijacking through XSS attacks. Combined with the disabled auto-escaping vulnerability, an attacker can steal or manipulate any user's session.
findings.evidence:
```python
storage = RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False)
```
This allows JavaScript access to AIOHTTP_SESSION cookie, enabling attacks like: `alert(document.cookie)` after session fixation.
findings.recommendation: Change to `httponly=True` (the secure default). This prevents JavaScript from accessing the cookie, limiting exposure to server-side session theft attacks. Also implement session rotation on login/logout to prevent session fixation attacks.

findings.title: Disabled CSRF Protection
findings.description: CSRF middleware is commented out, leaving the application vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery attacks. Attackers can trick authenticated users into performing unintended actions (creating students, courses, reviews, changing grades) by embedding requests in third-party websites. For example, an attacker can create a website with `` to create a student account when a logged-in admin visits.
findings.evidence:
```python
app = Application(
    debug=True,
    middlewares=[
        session_middleware,
        # csrf_middleware,  # <-- COMMENTED OUT, DISABLED
        error_middleware,
    ]
)
```
Although csrf_middleware is defined in middlewares.py, it's never registered in the application middleware stack.
findings.recommendation: Uncomment the csrf_middleware line and ensure CSRF tokens are validated on all state-changing operations (POST, PUT, DELETE). Include the CSRF token in all forms: `<input type='hidden' name='_csrf_token' value='{{ csrf_token() }}'>`

findings.title: Missing Authorization Checks on Sensitive Endpoints
findings.description: Multiple endpoints that modify sensitive data lack authorization decorators: (1) POST /students/ creates students without requiring authentication, (2) POST /courses/ creates courses without requiring authentication, (3) POST /courses/{course_id}/review creates reviews without requiring authentication, (4) POST /students/{student_id}/evaluate/{course_id} creates grades without admin role validation. Attackers can bypass the UI to directly invoke these endpoints and perform unauthorized actions.
findings.evidence:
```python
@template('students.jinja2')
async def students(request: Request):  # <-- No @authorize() decorator
    if request.method == 'POST':
        data = await request.post()
        await Student.create(conn, data['name'])  # <-- Any user can create students

async def courses(request: Request):  # <-- No @authorize() decorator
    if request.method == 'POST':
        await Course.create(conn, ...)  # <-- Any user can create courses

async def review(request: Request):  # <-- No @authorize() decorator
    if request.method == 'POST':
        await Review.create(...)  # <-- Any user can create reviews

async def evaluate(request: Request):  # <-- No @authorize() decorator
    # No check for admin role
    await Mark.create(...)  # <-- Any user can create grades
```
findings.recommendation: Add @authorize() and @authorize(ensure_admin=True) decorators to endpoints that require authentication or admin role: Apply `@authorize()` to students/POST, courses/POST, review/POST. Apply `@authorize(ensure_admin=True)` to evaluate/POST. Verify authorization checks are enforced at the API layer, not just in the UI templates.

findings.title: Hardcoded Database Credentials in Configuration File
findings.description: Database password is hardcoded in the configuration file. If this file is accidentally committed to version control, exposed in backups, or accessed through directory traversal, an attacker gains direct database access with full read/write privileges. The plaintext password allows attackers to compromise the entire database containing user credentials, student records, and grades.
findings.evidence:
```yaml
db:
  user: postgres
  password: postgres  # <-- Hardcoded plaintext password
  host: postgres
  port: 5432
  database: sqli
```
findings.recommendation: Load database credentials from environment variables instead of configuration files. Use: `db_password = os.environ.get('DB_PASSWORD')` or a secrets management system like HashiCorp Vault. Keep config/dev.yaml out of version control using .gitignore. Use separate configuration files for development (git-tracked with placeholder values) and production (managed securely via environment variables or secrets managers).
